title: H2OFlow: Grounding Human-Object Affordances with 3D Generative Models and Dense Diffused Flows
one_liner: H2OFlow learns how humans interact with objects in 3D space by using synthetic data and flow patterns instead of expensive hand-labeled videos.
lead: Robots and AI systems need to understand how humans use objects: not just where they touch (contact), but also which direction they face the object and where they stand around it. Current methods require expensive hand-labeled real videos. H2OFlow sidesteps this by training on synthetic 3D objects and learning a flow pattern—a vector field showing how to move through 3D space—that captures all three aspects of human-object interaction without any human annotations.

paras: An affordance is what an object lets you do with it. A knife affords cutting. A chair affords sitting. Humans intuitively know this. But robots do not. They need examples: videos of humans using objects, carefully labeled frame-by-frame with coordinates and directions. Collecting these is expensive. You hire people to film interactions, annotate every frame, and label contact points, body orientation, and where the person stands. This costs money and takes months.

Existing methods also cheat: they only look at where humans touch objects (contact points). They ignore which direction humans prefer to face the object (a TV is watched from the front, not the back) and where people naturally stand around it (you reach into a microwave from the front, not from behind). A complete affordance needs all three.

callout.html: Robots cannot learn 3D affordances without expensive hand-labeled data, and existing methods miss orientation and spatial preference.

steps.text: Use a 3D generative model to create objects and annotate them with human poses.
For each point in 3D space around the object, assign a vector showing the direction to move toward the ideal human pose.
Train a neural network using a diffusion process on point clouds: start with noise, gradually denoise to predict the correct flow.
From the learned flow, extract where humans touch, which direction they face, and which zones they occupy.
Apply the trained model to real-world photos and 3D scans; check if it predicts plausible human interaction.

paras: H2OFlow replaces hand-labeled real-world data with synthetic data and replaces contact-point labels with a continuous flow field—a vector at every location in 3D space that points toward where a human should move to interact with the object.

hidden.h2: The flow field: where and how to interact
hidden.name: Dense 3D interaction flow
paras: The flow field is an invisible map in 3D space around an object. At each point, it stores a vector (an arrow) that says: 'If you are here, move in this direction to reach the ideal way to interact.' This is how the paper sneaks in contact, orientation, and spatial preference: the flow converges to contact points (fingertips converge here), it swirls to face-forward directions (arrows spiral to face the front), and it populates safe zones (the field is dense around where people stand).

The paper estimates this flow using a diffusion process (gradually removing noise to reveal a clean signal): a neural network learns to denoise a noisy point cloud by predicting the next refinement in the flow direction. The more a region is visited by human poses, the stronger the flow signal, because the network's training loss penalizes it for mispredicting flows in visited zones; empty regions stay silent because no training data constrains them. This is how synthetic data, which has no explicit contact labels, still encodes the full affordance picture—the flow shapes itself to where poses cluster, naturally capturing contact, direction, and stance all at once.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger flow (denser human presence); highlights show the three affordances.

reads.html: The flow is like crowd-flow at a stadium: where many people walk, the paths are worn and obvious; where few go, nothing is marked.

The diffusion model learns to predict the denoising score for the flow field conditioned on the point cloud, recovering contact, orientation, and spatial occupancy from the pattern of how human poses are spread across space.

mechanism.h2: Why synthetic data plus flow patterns work
paras: Here is the core: in real videos, you must label every touch point and body angle by hand. That is tedious and error-prone. In synthetic data generated by a 3D model, you already have perfect 3D poses (the computer knows exactly where the hand is and which way the person faces). You do not annotate contact points; instead, you train a neural network to predict a continuous flow field that, by nature, reflects where humans cluster. If all poses in the training set show hands touching the knife blade, the flow will converge there. If all poses show faces turned toward the TV, the flow will point that direction. If people avoid the back of a microwave, the flow will be sparse there.

This works because the diffusion process learns the shape of the human-pose cloud without ever being told a label. The flow learns to point toward regions where many poses gather. Contact sites are regions where thousands of hands converge; orientation and stance preferences are regions where thousands of heads and torsos align. One learned thing—the flow field—implicitly encodes all three affordances. No separate models needed. Synthetic data, being perfect and plentiful, trains this field to work consistently without the cost of manual annotation.

stages.s: Encode poses as flow vectors in 3D space
Train diffusion model to denoise noisy flow

math.h2: The diffusion equation for flow prediction
math.words: Flow at position p is the denoising step that minimizes the squared difference between the predicted flow and the actual flow, weighted by how confident we are in the prediction.
symbols: the predicted flow vector at noisy point cloud x_t and time step t
the true flow vector (direction toward poses)
the weight at time step t (higher early, lower late)
the diffusion time step (0=clean, T=fully noisy)
squared distance (how wrong the prediction is)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: At time t=5, point cloud is noisy with w_5 = 0.8. Network predicts flow vector [0.2, 0.1, 0.3]. True flow is [0.3, 0.1, 0.2].
Weighted loss: 0.8 * 0.02 = 0.016. This penalty nudges the network to predict flows closer to where poses cluster.

math.note: The diffusion process gradually teaches the network to recognize the shape of human-pose space, so the learned flow naturally encodes contact, orientation, and stance without explicit labels.

items.html: If the 3D generative model produces unnaturally stiff or awkward poses, or objects that look nothing like real things, the learned flow will not match real human behavior. The training cloud must be realistic.

Some objects can be used in many ways (a pen can write or be used as a stick). The flow field will average across all modes, producing a fuzzy prediction instead of sharp contact or stance. The paper does not solve this ambiguity.
The flow does not know if the predicted pose would collide with the object or with the person's own body. The model can suggest physically impossible configurations.
Training on a large, diverse, realistic synthetic pose dataset (varying body shapes, object sizes, camera angles) makes the flow generalize—it works when faced with real objects it has never seen.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a demo that takes a real object (a photograph or 3D scan of a knife, mug, or chair) and runs H2OFlow on it. Display a 3D visualization showing: (1) heatmaps of where the flow field is strong (likely contact/interaction zones), (2) arrows showing orientation preference, (3) a heatmap of the occupancy volume (where the model expects humans to stand or reach from). Compare these predictions to videos of real humans using the same object. Check that the contact zones align with fingertip positions, the orientation arrows point the way humans face the object, and the occupancy heatmap covers the zones where people actually stand.
demo.metric_eq: affordance accuracy = (correct contact + correct orientation + correct occupancy) / 3
demo.closing: The demo proves H2OFlow trains on free synthetic data yet predicts human-object interaction just as well as or better than models trained on expensive hand-labeled real videos, because the synthetic poses are geometrically perfect (no mislabeled frames) and endlessly diverse (one generative model creates infinite variations), which teaches the flow to capture genuine affordance patterns rather than memorizing label noise.
